chapters.title: Where Does Morality Come From?
chapters.sourcePressure: The chapter asks where morality comes from, weighing nativism, blank-slate empiricism, reasoning-heavy development, cross-cultural variation, and moral dumbfounding.
chapters.coreMove: Catch a moral verdict before the reason arrives, then ask what native and cultural machinery may have produced it.
chapters.commonMisread: Morality is either fully taught by adults or fully reasoned out by smart people.

chapters.title: The Intuitive Dog and Its Rational Tail
chapters.sourcePressure: The chapter makes the intuition-first claim directly: moral reasoning often justifies and persuades after intuition has already moved.
chapters.coreMove: Treat a moral reason as an advocate's brief until you know which intuition hired it.
chapters.commonMisread: Feelings are irrational mistakes and reasons are always neutral truth-seeking tools.

chapters.title: Elephants Rule
chapters.sourcePressure: The chapter deepens the rider-elephant mechanism by showing why reflective control has limited command over entrenched intuitions and habits.
chapters.coreMove: Steer the elephant by changing conditions and incentives before asking the rider for a speech.
chapters.commonMisread: Self-control means thinking harder until the correct choice wins.

chapters.title: Vote for Me (Here's Why)
chapters.sourcePressure: The chapter moves from private moral justification to public persuasion, ally recruitment, reputation defense, and political-style explanation.
chapters.coreMove: Listen for what a reason is trying to sell and whom it is trying to recruit.
chapters.commonMisread: Argument is mainly a courtroom search for the cleanest truth.

chapters.title: Beyond WEIRD Morality
chapters.sourcePressure: The chapter turns from WEIRD moral assumptions toward a broader cross-cultural moral range beyond harm and fairness.
chapters.coreMove: Before judging a moral reaction as irrational, ask whether a non-WEIRD moral concern is doing the work.
chapters.commonMisread: Harm and fairness exhaust morality, and every other concern is prejudice or noise.

chapters.title: Taste Buds of the Righteous Mind
chapters.sourcePressure: The chapter makes moral plurality concrete through the taste-buds metaphor and several kinds of moral trigger.
chapters.coreMove: Name the moral receptor that fired before arguing about whether the reaction is reasonable.
chapters.commonMisread: Different moral reactions are just preferences with moral clothing.

chapters.title: The Moral Foundations of Politics
chapters.sourcePressure: The chapter applies multiple moral foundations to political life and treats disagreement as different moral emphases.
chapters.coreMove: Translate a political claim into the moral foundations it is activating before deciding what it means.
chapters.commonMisread: The other side has no moral concerns, only selfishness or stupidity.

chapters.title: The Conservative Advantage
chapters.sourcePressure: The chapter argues for a politically sensitive conservative advantage in moral-register breadth, not blanket moral superiority.
chapters.coreMove: Separate breadth of moral vocabulary from virtue, truth, or policy quality.
chapters.commonMisread: Conservatives are morally better, or liberals care about almost nothing.

chapters.title: Why Are We So Groupish?
chapters.sourcePressure: The chapter reopens morality through groupishness, multilevel selection, and the tension between self-interest and group-binding tendencies.
chapters.coreMove: Hold selfish motives and group-binding motives in the same picture instead of reducing one to the other.
chapters.commonMisread: Groupishness is just tribalism with a nicer name.

chapters.title: The Hive Switch
chapters.sourcePressure: The chapter explains conditions under which people shift into group-minded coordination through the hive switch.
chapters.coreMove: Notice the cues that move people from private calculation into shared-body coordination.
chapters.commonMisread: Crowds make people irrational and that is the whole story.

chapters.title: Religion Is a Team Sport
chapters.sourcePressure: The chapter interprets religion as a group-binding institution that coordinates ritual, cohesion, and shared moral life without reducing religion to one function.
chapters.coreMove: Evaluate religion by the team behavior it organizes as well as by the beliefs it states.
chapters.commonMisread: Religion is only private doctrine, only deception, or only tribal aggression.

chapters.title: Can't We All Disagree More Constructively?
chapters.sourcePressure: The closing chapter synthesizes intuition-first judgment, moral foundations, group binding, and politics/religion into more constructive disagreement.
chapters.coreMove: Enter the other person's moral matrix before answering their argument.
chapters.commonMisread: Understanding the other side should make disagreement disappear.
